# How Politics Percolates Through Science Assessment

Dahyun Choi1→

1Department of Politics, Princeton University, Princeton 08540, USA.

→Corresponding author. Email: dahyunc@princeton.edu

Scientiﬁc research has been considered a primary source of information for improving policy outcomes, but its use is inevitably intertwined with political considerations. Using a comprehensive dataset of peer-reviewed journal articles evaluated for the National Ambient Air Quality Standards, this paper examines the trade-o! between partisan bias and evidence quality in internal science evaluation by government agencies. I ﬁnd that the integration of science into policymaking is guided by a pursuit of expertise but biased in favor of the presidential administration. The evaluation of low-quality studies is more susceptible to partisan bias, while high-quality studies remain relatively una!ected. This work not only provides an empirical examination of long-standing questions about how information is used by politically divergent factions but also illuminates the pathways through which academic research connects the contours of evidence-based policymaking.

Today, science is heralded as the cornerstone of evidence-based policymaking. Federal agencies in the United States emphasize science as a primary input to their regulatory processes, convening scientiﬁc advisory boards, having scientists to craft regulations, and granting approvals based on scientiﬁc evidence (1, 2). These mechanisms underscore a commitment to integrating expertise into the development of policies that address public welfare, environmental or health risks (3–5). Yet, how much, then, should we trust the application of science to the policymaking process? Policymakers often face competing pressures, where scientiﬁc evidence can serve not only as a tool for addressing complex problems but also as a strategic instrument to justify preordained policy decisions amid political and economic constraints (6, 7). Grounded on the literature on partisan bias and bureaucratic implementation (8–10), this paper investigates the inﬂuence of political considerations on the review process of scientiﬁc studies by federal agencies.

## Theory and research questions

The impact of political inﬂuence on bureaucratic performance has been a widely studied topic (11–15). A large body of work has found evidence of partisan bias in the implementation of public policy (8, 16–18), often through the politicization or centralization of bureaucracy (9, 10, 19, 20).

These ﬁndings raise critical questions about how bureaucrats obtain and use expertise, as their regulatory behavior is often shaped by political priorities. While expertise is vital for informed policy decisions (21–26), the incentive to align agency actions with political priorities (27–29) can lead to regulatory behavior that reﬂects partisan preferences in the use and acquisition of expertise.

This tension is particularly concerning for agencies that rely on scientiﬁc studies to address complex issues such as air quality or drinking water safety, as these studies are inherently used in ways that involve decisions about which knowledge is selectively interpreted or emphasized, and how it aligns with political interests (30, 31). To formalize this dynamic, consider the case where bureaucrats evaluate scientiﬁc research for policy formulation. ## Design and results

To further illustrate the previous section’s implications, I construct a comprehensive dataset of peerreviewed journal articles that underwent full-text review for the Integrated Science Assessment for Ozone and Related Photochemical Oxidants (ISA) under the National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS), spanning both Democratic and Republican administrations. Under the Obama Administration, the EPA lowered the NAAQS limit from 75 parts per billion to 70 parts per billion, averaged over an eight-hour period (33). Since then, public health advocates have pushed for lower ozone levels, citing greater impacts on at-risk populations, but the Trump administration declined stricter limits (34). According to the EPA, these decisions were based on an extensive scientiﬁc review (35). The amendments to the Clean Air Act speciﬁcally mandate that standards must reﬂect “scientiﬁc knowledge.” In line with this directive, the EPA publishes the ISA to evaluate the strength of evidence regarding the adverse impacts of pollutants on human health and public welfare (see Fig. S2 for a detailed overview of the ISA process). Notably, the ISA document explicitly states the following on its second page:

The ISA provides a concise review, synthesis, and evaluation of the most policy-relevant science to serve as a scientiﬁc foundation for the review of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS).

My analysis relies on two key components: (i) the turnover of the administration in power, and (ii) a quality measure for each scientiﬁc study, including those that received full-text review but were ultimately excluded from the policymaking process. I construct a scientiﬁc text-based measure to assess the relationship of studies to administrators’ political strategies—speciﬁcally, the likelihood that a study supports the linkage between environmental risks (e.g., increased ozone exposure) and public health outcomes (e.g., cancer or expiratory volume). This measure captures whether a study aligns with and bolsters the administration’s regulatory policy agenda, particularly when the administration is pursuing strong regulatory actions. It is unlikely to be correlated with study quality, as changes in administration represent an exogenous shock unrelated to the circumstances under which scholars originally produced the paper (see SM section S1.5 for more details). I then collect two measures of study quality using WOS: (1) ﬁeld citation ratio and (2) citation count normalized by subject category and publication year within my sample, as the impact of each study can vary across disciplines and time periods independently of publication quality (36). For normalized citation counts, 8,059 studies are included, while 7,202 studies are considered for the ﬁeld citation ratio, as some category-publication years lack enough comparable studies to assess the impact (see SM section S1.4 for details). Given these, the intuition underlying my empirical work is as follows: if politics permeates the way that science is used for policymaking, then studies closely related to administration policy strategies should receive better evaluation regardless of their quality. If science is also used for expertise acquisition, then the e!ect of partisan bias should di!er for high and low-quality studies; the impact of partisanship would decrease as study quality increases.

To appreciate the magnitude of this e!ect, I examine how sensitive the EPA’s evaluation decisions are to changes in study quality. As shown in Fig. S7, a study’s likelihood of being cited increases linearly with its quality. A regression of study evaluation on study quality, indicates that a study’s likelihood of being cited in the ﬁnal ISAs increases by 16 percentage points for every 100-point increase in the ﬁeld citation ratio and by 52 percentage points for every 10 normalized citation count increase in quality (see SM Tables S9 and S10). Comparing this with the coe”cient in column 4 suggests that being evaluated by an administration whose policy strategies align with a study’s implications increases the likelihood of the study being cited in the ﬁnal ISAs by an amount equivalent to the increase expected from 2.69 additional normalized counts (about 2.77 standard deviations) or an 87.5-point increase in the ﬁeld citation ratio (approximately 2.23 standard

This signiﬁcant e!ect suggests that when the evaluation of quality is tricky, political considerations regarding how a study can be leveraged to beneﬁt the administration may play an outsized role in the use of science. *Table 1 provides initial evidence that the evaluation process is not solely driven by obtaining higher-quality information. If the review process were unbiased and solely focused on identifying high-quality studies, it would result in a greater proportion of related studies surpassing the evaluation threshold, but it would not a!ect the average evaluations of partisan-aligned studies. To investigate how the impact of partisanship varies by study quality, I analyze the relationship between study quality and the probability of being cited using actual data. Studies are categorized into two groups: those related to the administration’s policy agenda and those not related. The ﬁrst group includes studies reviewed for the 2013 ISA (under a Democratic administration) with a probability greater than 0.5 of a link between climate risk and public health, as well as studies reviewed for the 2020 ISA (under a Republican administration) that have a probability of a link lower than 0.5. The second group consists of all other studies. This categorization is designed to examine how partisan bias inﬂuences the EPA’s evaluation decisions, contingent on the relevance and perceived quality of the studies. Fig.2 shows the likelihood of a study being cited in the ﬁnal ISAs, controlling for study-level characteristics.*

The estimated relationship between study quality and evaluation decisions for related and unrelated studies suggests that both partisan bias and the demand for high-quality evidence inﬂuence ISAs. The impact of relatedness increases with study quality: high-quality studies are more likely to be cited compared to low-quality studies in both groups, highlighting the role of expertise. However, if the process were unbiased, we would expect low-quality works to be penalized equally across both related and unrelated groups. Instead, the results reveal that low-quality studies tend to beneﬁt disproportionately from being aligned with the ruling administration’s agenda, while this advantage diminishes for high-quality studies.

To clarify this pattern, Table 2 divides the main sample into quartiles based on study quality and separately estimates the impact of partisan bias on each subset. Column 1 of Table 2 replicates the results from Column 4 of Table 1, showing the impact of partisanship on the entire sample. Columns 2–5 conﬁrm the pattern illustrated in Fig.2. Speciﬁcally, I ﬁnd no evidence of partisan bias in the top quartile of study quality, in contrast to a large and signiﬁcant for studies in the bottom quartiles. The impact of partisanship gradually decreases as study quality increases, indicating that higher-quality studies are less susceptible to partisan bias compared to lower-quality studies. This pattern remains consistent across two di!erent measures of quality. Table S12 presents the full results for Panel A, including control variables, while Table S13 reports the complete results for Panel B. This pattern is clearer with binary classiﬁcation rather than continuous predictive probability, as shown in Table S19 and S20, and is robust to doubly robust bias correction. To explore the pattern at a ﬁner level, Fig. S15 plots the estimated e!ect of partisan bias by deciles of study quality.

## Discussion

A potential concern with my analysis is the strategic selection of studies chosen for full-text review. One might suspect that the pool of studies may have been curated to align with the administration’s political interests, resulting in limited variation among the studies selected for full review and potentially excluding high-quality studies that do not align with the ruling administration’s preferred policy agenda. To address this concern, I examine the entire universe of studies, including both those that underwent a full-text review and those that were identiﬁed in the literature search but excluded prior to the full-text review during the 2020 ISA process, in SM section S1.9.3. I present evidence using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests to demonstrate that the quality of studies between these two groups does not di!er. Additionally, the studies selected for full-text review are not more favorable to the ruling administration’s policy agenda compared to those excluded before the fulltext review. In the meantime, the screening process reduced the number of subject categories from 95 to 64, likely to identify the most relevant topics rather than to introduce political manipulation or quality-based bias, considering the large volume of academic publications.

In SM section S1.9.4, I present an alternative regression model inspired by Equation 1. If the theoretical predictions hold, we would expect a negative coe”cient for the variable capturing the penalty from partisan misalignment and a positive coe”cient for the variable representing the gains from quality. Table S27 reports outcomes consistent with these predictions across all models. In SM section S1.8, I explore the mechanisms underlying these patterns by examining the selection of individuals involved in the ISA process. Additionally, in SM section S1.8.2, I provide further analyses using the studies recommended in the Clean Air Scientiﬁc Advisory Committee (CASAC) / public comments for the 2020 ISAs. While the quality of studies recommended by CASAC/public comments and other studies does not di!er signiﬁcantly overall, Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests indicate that Prob(link) values for CASAC/public comment studies are smaller, aligning more closely with the ruling administration’s policy strategies. Table S15 shows these studies are more likely to be cited in the ﬁnal ISA.

By examining the trade-o!s between evidence quality and partisan bias in the context of EPA science assessments, this study contributes to our understanding of the role of expertise and political bias in American policymaking (22,24), while highlighting the uncertainty and incompleteness in the application of science (37). Although this study does not claim that the conclusions regarding partisan bias and expertise will always apply to other contexts, such as judicial decision-making or policy domains like ﬁnance, the empirical setting of this paper is particularly signiﬁcant, as the agency in question is notably subject to political inﬂuences and addresses issues that inherently require scientiﬁc and technical evidence.
